issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
issues.explanation: Water/flooding triggers are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another in a car accident, given the rest of the profile centers on crash-related and guilt/shame themes. This trigger introduces a different threat context without support from memory or appraisal items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Feelings: Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Feelings' is internally incoherent as worded: 'Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion' describes the opposite of avoidance. Within the maladaptive strategies node, it directly conflicts with an avoidance strategy.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body
issues.explanation: 'Body Unreliable' fits poorly with the rest of the profile for a perpetration-type accident trauma in which the patient's appraisals otherwise center on guilt, humiliation, and shattered beliefs. There are no memory, trigger, or strategy items suggesting bodily injury, panic/somatic threat, or physical incapacity to support this appraisal.

vignette: Ravi, a 42-year-old South Asian man and tax inspector, has been grappling with intense guilt and shame since he accidentally caused serious injury to another person. The traumatic event remains vividly etched in his mind: it was late afternoon when Ravi, on his way home from work, lost control of his car on an icy road and collided with another vehicle head-on. He remembers the sound of shattering glass, the screeching brakes, and the horrified screams from within the other car. The image of the injured driver being carried away by paramedics has been haunting him ever since. Ravi's triggers are particularly potent in his daily life as a tax inspector. Whenever he drives past the scene of the accident or sees cars hit by others on television, he feels an overwhelming sense of panic and guilt. Similarly, attending funerals or even watching grief-related scenes on TV makes him relive those traumatic moments. He avoids talking about the event entirely because it brings back too many painful memories. Ravi's coping mechanisms have become increasingly maladaptive over time. When these triggers are activated, he tells himself that he deserves to suffer for what happened. This form of punishment thinking is his way of making sense of his guilt and shame. Additionally, he often reminds himself that the situation could have been worse as a means of self-soothing, but this only reinforces his belief that he failed to protect others adequately. His memory of the event is fragmented and incomplete. During moments when he recalls the accident, Ravi sometimes hears sounds in his head that echo those from the day of the incident. However, some parts of the memory are clear while others remain entirely blank. This inconsistency makes him feel like he can only remember pieces of what happened, which exacerbates his sense of failure and humiliation. Ravi's negative appraisals have taken a significant toll on his mental well-being. He feels permanently humiliated by the event and believes that his perception of how the world works has been irrevocably destroyed. This shattered worldview is closely tied to his belief that he should have protected others but failed in doing so. These beliefs have intensified over time, leading him to suppress thoughts about the trauma even more rigorously. The memory gaps and auditory recollections often trigger intense anxiety and further reinforce Ravi’s negative appraisals. When he hears certain sounds or sees images reminiscent of the crash, his mind spirals into a downward spiral of self-blame and guilt. This vicious cycle has become increasingly difficult for him to break, as each trigger leads to more punishing thoughts about himself. Ravi's maladaptive strategies further perpetuate this negative cycle. His tendency to punish himself by believing he deserves suffering only deepens his sense of humiliation and failure. Similarly, the more he suppresses thoughts about the trauma, the more vividly the memories return, often with a renewed intensity that triggers additional anxiety and guilt. The accumulation of these experiences has taken a toll on Ravi's work life as well. He finds it increasingly difficult to drive or even commute by car due to the fear of encountering similar situations. This has led him to avoid certain routes and modes of transportation, making his daily commute more stressful and time-consuming. His relationships have also been affected; he struggles to share his feelings with his wife, who is growing concerned about his increasing isolation. Ultimately, it was a combination of these mounting difficulties that finally prompted Ravi to seek help. He hopes to find ways to cope with the guilt and shame without resorting to self-punishment or avoidance. What frightens him most is the possibility that he will never be able to reconcile what happened and move forward with his life. Despite this fear, Ravi is determined to address these issues before they further erode his sense of self and daily functioning. In summary, Ravi’s clinical portrait reveals a deeply intertwined set of traumatic triggers, maladaptive coping strategies, fragmented memories, and negative appraisals that have created a self-reinforcing cycle. The most pressing concern for him is finding ways to break this cycle and begin the process of healing from his trauma.
